## 6. Climatology — Polar Night (mid-January)

- **Light:** Above the Arctic Circle the area is in **polar night** — near-continuous darkness through mid-January, with only brief, dim civil twilight near local noon in the southern Norwegian Sea and none at the Svalbard latitudes. Operations are effectively round-the-clock night.
- **Sea state and weather:** Frequent North Atlantic / Barents storm tracks drive **sea state 4–6** across the open corridors, with higher states in passing systems; usable **weather windows are narrow** and short-fused.
- **Icing and ice edge:** **Superstructure and rotor icing** is a persistent hazard for surface ships and helicopters; the **northern Barents ice edge** advances and shifts through the season, constraining access to the Svalbard approaches and complicating any operation north and east of Bear Island.
- **Temperature/visibility:** Sub-zero air and sea-spray, reduced visibility in snow showers and sea smoke.

## 7. Operational Effects of the Environment

- **Surface operations:** SS 4–6 and icing reduce small-boat, davit, and flight-deck availability and slow the cable-repair ship, lengthening restoration timelines and the windows in which escort and protection must be sustained.
- **Air/ISR operations:** Icing, low ceilings, and darkness constrain MPA and helicopter sorties and degrade some EO/IR collection; high-altitude ISR is less weather-limited but must contend with the PNT environment.
- **Undersea/seabed forensics:** Surface sea state limits the launch, tow, and recovery of seabed-survey and acoustic systems (T-AGOS / ROV operations), narrowing the forensics windows at Cut Sites A and B.
- **PNT-degraded navigation:** The polar-night, high-latitude environment already stresses navigation (poor celestial reference, high-latitude compass error); layered onto the **GPS/PNT jamming and AIS spoofing** over Finnmark and the Svalbard approaches, this makes precise station-keeping over a cut site, corridor patrol, and de-confliction of friendly surface and air tracks materially harder, and elevates the value of alternate-navigation and counter-EW measures. The EMS and PNT picture, and the SPACECOM coordination seam, are developed in `11_Annexes.md` (Cyber/EW and Climatology annexes) and the running estimates (`14_Running_Estimates.md`).

- **Polar-night climatology.** Mid-January polar night above the Arctic Circle: near-continuous darkness, sea state 4–6, persistent superstructure icing, and an intermittent ice edge in the northern Barents. Severe-weather windows constrain surface, air, and — critically — cable-repair operations, narrowing the periods in which protection and forensics can occur and lengthening restoration timelines.
- **EMS / PNT environment.** Sustained Kola-based GPS/PNT jamming and AIS spoofing degrade navigation across Finnmark and the Svalbard approaches, peaking 11 JAN. The footprint affects friendly receivers as well as civil and adversary ones; degraded PNT is simultaneously an indicator to be characterized and a constraint on the forces conducting protection and seabed forensics.
- **Undersea acoustic conditions.** Polar-front and marginal-ice-zone gradients, seasonal layering, and shallow-shelf reverberation complicate the passive-acoustic and seabed-forensic picture; they raise the difficulty of localizing a subsurface contact (e.g., B-90 Vologda) and of distinguishing a deliberate seabed act from an anchor- or trawl-induced fault.

## 6. Non-Force Resources

- **Contracted cable-repair ship** — commercial vessel under contract to the cable operators; sets the restoration timeline and is the protected unit for the escort task at Cut Site B (Boreal Connect). Schedule and on-station windows are weather-dependent.
- **Commercial cable operators and the HVDC interconnector operator** — own the fault data and restoration prioritization; central to both protection and forensics; not under military control.
- **NATO MARCOM Critical Undersea Infrastructure (CUI) Coordination Cell, Northwood** — the Alliance node coordinating the CUI-protection picture across national and NATO contributions; the principal coordination interface between the US national effort, SNMG1, and Allied national forces. The Cell synchronizes surveillance and de-conflicts the multinational protection effort but does not exercise command over national forces.

- **Phase I (Set / Deter):** flow the apportioned maritime and ISR force forward; establish a subsurface-inclusive maritime domain-awareness picture; integrate with the NATO MARCOM CUI Cell and the Norwegian Joint Headquarters; establish PNT-resilient operations with USSPACECOM.
- **Phase II (Protect / Attribute):** surveil and protect CUI; escort cable-repair operations; detect, track, and shadow suspect vessels; conduct seabed/acoustic forensics in support of attribution; develop deterrent-signaling options for decision.

## 3. Critical Undersea Infrastructure (Norwegian and Barents Seas)

Four seabed systems define the critical-infrastructure picture. As is typical of modern subsea cables, the telecom systems are shared-carriage: alongside civilian internet and data they transport managed capacity for institutional customers.

- **Svalbard Link — SVL-1 / SVL-2.** A **twin-pair** fiber system connecting **Longyearbyen** to the mainland landing at **Harstad** (68.80N, 16.54E). SVL carries Svalbard and SvalSat connectivity — civil internet and the satellite ground-station data noted at §2.2 — and, as managed transport on the same pair, a portion of **allied military-communications** traffic and **financial-clearing / settlement** data routed northbound. The pair is engineered for mutual redundancy: each fiber can carry the residual load if the other faults. **SVL-2 was severed 07 JAN** (Cut Site A, vicinity 76.5N 014.0E, in the Svalbard approaches); **SVL-1 now carries degraded but not fully severed** Svalbard/SvalSat connectivity, the redundancy gone.
- **Boreal Connect.** A **trans-Atlantic** data cable transiting the **Norwegian Sea** on the **Norway–Iceland–North America** route. Like SVL, Boreal Connect carries civilian internet and data plus managed allied military-communications transport and a share of **financial-clearing** traffic between European and North American nodes. It registered a **partial fault 09 JAN** (Cut Site B, vicinity 67.5N 002.0E).
- **Nordkapp Data Link (NDL).** Coastal fiber running along the **Finnmark** coast, serving northern Norwegian communities and connecting onward to the broader national network. It registered **intermittent faults 11 JAN**, coincident with a stronger episode of GPS/PNT jamming along the coast.
- **Arctic Bridge HVDC.** A high-voltage direct-current **power interconnector** segment in the **Norwegian Sea**, tying northern generation and grids into the wider European market (§1.5). It experienced a **protective trip 12 JAN**, with the operator's preliminary assessment consistent with **suspected anchor-drag damage**.

The systems are mutually independent in routing but concentrate in the same corridors and chokepoints (see `06_Critical_Geography.md`). The loss of redundancy across the telecom pair, and the breadth of traffic each cable carries, mean the consequence of any further cut rises sharply.

- **07 JAN — Cut Site A.** SVL-2, one of the twin Svalbard Link fibers (Longyearbyen–Harstad), is **severed** near the Svalbard approaches (Cut Site A, vicinity 76.5N 014.0E). Loss of SVL-2 degrades, but does not sever, connectivity from Longyearbyen and the Svalbard Satellite Station; SVL-1 carries the residual load. GS Pomor's AIS shows an extended gap bracketing the fault timeframe in the broader Svalbard approaches.
- **09 JAN — Cut Site B.** The trans-Atlantic data cable Boreal Connect (Norway–Iceland–North America) registers a **partial fault** in the Norwegian Sea (Cut Site B, vicinity 67.5N 002.0E). The shadow-fleet bulk carrier MV Kola Trader is the nearest tracked commercial vessel to the corridor in the preceding days, with an AIS gap of several hours over the relevant segment.
- **11 JAN — Nordkapp Data Link.** The coastal fiber along Finnmark (NDL) registers **intermittent faults**, coincident with a renewed and stronger episode of GPS/PNT jamming along the Finnmark coast. The simultaneity complicates fault localization and is itself assessed as a possible masking effect.
- **12 JAN — Arctic Bridge HVDC.** A segment of the Arctic Bridge HVDC power interconnector in the Norwegian Sea experiences a **protective trip**; operator preliminary assessment is consistent with suspected anchor-drag damage. The crude tanker MV Arktika Star transited the general area with an AIS gap in the preceding 24 hours; an anchor-drag mechanism is consistent with both a deliberate act and a genuine accident, and the two cannot yet be distinguished from the available data.

- **LOE 1 — Protect CUI.** *Main effort initially.* Surveillance and protective presence over the cable/interconnector corridors; escort and protect cable-repair operations; prioritize by **military-communications dependency**, not by cable length or commercial value.

#### (d) National-Level Restraints and Constraints

The following are directed and are not waivable below the National Command Authority:

- Operate below the threshold of armed conflict at all times.
- **Do not invoke or imply NATO Article 5.** US action supports the Article 4 consultative process and Norway as host/lead; this order directs the US national chain only.
- **No kinetic action against Russian state vessels.** Interaction with suspect or Russian state vessels is limited to lawful detection, tracking, shadowing, and presence.
- **No entry into Russian territorial waters.**
- **No boarding or seizure of any vessel in international waters absent a positive legal determination and a separate grant of authority.** Cable damage in the high seas and the Norwegian EEZ sits under flag-state jurisdiction and the limited enforcement regime of reference (e); the binding constraint is legal-jurisdictional.
- Comply with UNCLOS (reference (e)) and the Svalbard Treaty regime (reference (f)), including the demilitarization nuance constraining posture around the archipelago.
- **No public attribution release without National Command Authority and NATO coordination.** Contest, do not amplify, adversary deniability narratives.
- **RETAINED AT THE NCA:** approval of any deterrent action with offensive cyber effect; any use of force beyond unit self-defense; and any change to the posture or restraints above. CDR USEUCOM is the senior military planning authority and may plan, posture, and rehearse within the restraints of this order.

**Submarine-cable regime (UNCLOS).**
- UNCLOS **Art. 113** requires each state to make it a punishable offense for a vessel flying its flag, or a person subject to its jurisdiction, to break or injure a submarine cable willfully or by culpable negligence.
- **Art. 114** addresses liability of cable owners to one another; **Art. 115** provides for indemnity of vessels that sacrifice gear to avoid injuring a cable. The regime is principally one of flag-state penalty and inter-owner liability, not third-state enforcement.
- Enforcement therefore runs principally through **flag-state jurisdiction**. There is **no general coastal-state or third-state authority to board, search, seize, or divert a foreign-flagged vessel on the high seas or in the EEZ for cable damage** absent flag-state consent, a treaty basis, or another recognized exception.
- **Consequence.** For the faults at Cut Site A (Svalbard approaches) and Cut Site B (Norwegian Sea high seas), and for activity in the Norwegian EEZ, **US/Allied enforcement authority over cable damage in international waters is limited**. The binding constraint on interdiction is legal/jurisdictional, not military, and it persists even where the responsible vessel is identified.

**Svalbard Treaty regime.**
- The 1920 Svalbard Treaty confirms Norwegian sovereignty over the archipelago while granting treaty-party nationals equal economic access. Art. 9 constrains the use of the archipelago for "warlike purposes" and is the source of the demilitarization nuance that bounds military posture in and around Svalbard.
- Operations near the Svalbard approaches and the Longyearbyen landing — including any escort of repair operations on SVL — must account for this regime and for Russia's standing readiness to characterize Allied activity there as militarization. It is a deliberate legal seam, not a settled permission; coordinate posture with Norway as the sovereign and with the legal-determination track below.

**ROE / RUF summary (SILENT FATHOM ROE Supplement to CJCSI 3121.01B).**
- Inherent right of **unit and individual self-defense** always applies, including defense of accompanied repair and partner units.
- Posture toward Russian state vessels is **defensive**; **no kinetic action against Russian state vessels** and **no entry into Russian territorial waters**.
- **No boarding, seizure, or diversion of vessels in international waters absent a positive legal determination and granted authority.** Shadowing, querying on bridge-to-bridge, overt presence, and persistent ISR are permitted within standing guidance.
- All operations remain **below the threshold of armed conflict.** **Do not invoke or imply NATO Article 5.**
- Coordinate with Norway as host/lead and through the NAC consultative process; comply with UNCLOS and the Svalbard Treaty regime.
- **No public attribution release without NCA and NATO coordination.**

**Open decision item.** The **interdiction-authority determination** — whether, and on what basis, friendly forces may interdict GS Ladoga or a shadow-fleet vessel approaching the Bear Island Gap corridor in international waters / the Norwegian EEZ — is an **unresolved legal question** referred for determination. It is recorded as FFIR-2 and is a precondition for any action beyond shadowing at DP-1.

**Releasability.** Releasable to Norway and overt Allied contributors (UK, NATO MARCOM CUI Cell, SNMG1) on the CUI-protection and repair-escort lines per disclosure guidance; attribution-support and interdiction-option legal analysis held more closely pending the determination above.

Between 05 and 13 JAN 26, three subsea telecom/data cables and one HVDC power interconnector in the Norwegian and Barents Seas suffered near-simultaneous damage, coincident with sustained GPS/PNT jamming and AIS spoofing degrading navigation across Finnmark and the Svalbard approaches. A Russian-flagged GUGI-analog hydrographic/survey vessel (GS Pomor) and two shadow-fleet merchants (MV Arktika Star, MV Kola Trader) operated in or near the cable corridors during the window with extended, unexplained AIS gaps.

J2 assesses **with high confidence** that Russia possesses the deniable seabed and deep-submergence capability to conduct the observed damage, resident in the Northern Fleet's Main Directorate for Deep-Sea Research (GUGI-analog) on the Kola Peninsula. J2 assesses **with low confidence** the **intent** behind the incidents and holds **low confidence on conclusive attribution** — specifically whether the damage was directed by the Russian state, executed by a deniable proxy or shadow-fleet vessel acting at state behest, or in any individual case the product of an accident (anchor drag, trawl gear) of the kind that genuinely occurs in these waters. This capability-known / intent-and-attribution-uncertain split is the central analytic problem and motivates the collection priorities at §8.

### 3.2 Shadow-fleet and deniable maritime activity

MV Arktika Star (crude tanker) and MV Kola Trader (bulk carrier), both flags of convenience, exhibit the dark-activity profile (extended AIS gaps near the corridors, loitering inconsistent with their declared voyages) associated with Russia's shadow fleet. Their proximity to Cut Sites and to the HVDC corridor during the relevant windows is suggestive but, given the genuine density of commercial and fishing traffic and the prevalence of accidental anchor/trawl cable faults, is not by itself conclusive of a deliberate act or of state direction.

## 8. Adversary Center of Gravity (initial)

The adversary's operational center of gravity in this campaign is **deniability itself** — the layered ambiguity (research cover, accident-plausible mechanisms, flag-of-convenience merchants, EW masking, information-domain denial) that lets Russia demonstrate reach over Allied critical undersea infrastructure while denying the Alliance a confirmed, attributable act on which to base a collective response. Critical capabilities flow from the GUGI-analog seabed assets and the Kola EW grouping; critical requirements are research/commercial cover and the genuine baseline rate of accidental faults; the critical vulnerability is the forensic and multi-source fusion picture that, if developed, collapses the deniability and converts a plausible accident into an attributable act. This vulnerability is what the friendly attribution effort is designed to exploit.

## 9. Capabilities vs. Intent (confidence framing)

- **Capability — HIGH confidence.** Russia possesses the platforms (GUGI-analog survey vessels, B-90 *Vologda*), the seabed knowledge, the Kola EW assets, and the demonstrated doctrine to conduct deniable CUI interference and PNT degradation across the Norwegian and Barents Seas. This is not in analytic doubt.
- **Intent — LOW confidence.** Whether the campaign is intended to coerce Norway and the Alliance, condition the environment for future leverage, or probe response thresholds, is unresolved. The deliberate use of deniable means is itself consistent with an intent to stay below the level that compels collective defense.
- **Attribution — LOW confidence.** No single reporting stream resolves whether the damage was state-directed, executed by a deniable proxy/shadow-fleet vessel at state behest, or in any individual case genuinely accidental. The capability-known / intent-and-attribution-uncertain split is the central analytic problem and the driver of the collection priorities.

## 2. The Nine-Day Escalation Arc (05–13 JAN 26)

- **05–06 JAN.** Onset of intermittent GPS/PNT degradation and AIS anomalies over Finnmark and the Svalbard approaches, initially assessed as routine Kola-based EW activity within the observed seasonal pattern. GS Pomor departs the Kola area; AIS shows a normal coastal track before the first of several gaps.
- **07 JAN — Cut Site A.** SVL-2, one of the twin Svalbard Link fibers (Longyearbyen–Harstad), is **severed** near the Svalbard approaches (Cut Site A, vicinity 76.5N 014.0E). - **09 JAN — Cut Site B.** The trans-Atlantic data cable Boreal Connect (Norway–Iceland–North America) registers a **partial fault** in the Norwegian Sea (Cut Site B, vicinity 67.5N 002.0E). The shadow-fleet bulk carrier MV Kola Trader is the nearest tracked commercial vessel to the corridor in the preceding days, with an AIS gap of several hours over the relevant segment.
- **11 JAN — Nordkapp Data Link.** The coastal fiber along Finnmark (NDL) registers **intermittent faults**, coincident with a renewed and stronger episode of GPS/PNT jamming along the Finnmark coast. The simultaneity complicates fault localization and is itself assessed as a possible masking effect.
- **12 JAN — Arctic Bridge HVDC.** A segment of the Arctic Bridge HVDC power interconnector in the Norwegian Sea experiences a **protective trip**; operator preliminary assessment is consistent with suspected anchor-drag damage. The crude tanker MV Arktika Star transited the general area with an AIS gap in the preceding 24 hours; an anchor-drag mechanism is consistent with both a deliberate act and a genuine accident, and the two cannot yet be distinguished from the available data.

## 5. Protection

- **Running assessment.** The force must operate in a **PNT-degraded, EW-contested** environment — degraded GPS and spoofed AIS are assumed in the operating area. Protection spans three objects: the force, the cable-repair effort, and the **CUI itself** (prioritized by military-communications dependency). Force-protection posture is being set for a contested-navigation environment.
- **Key shortfalls / limiting factors.** **PNT degradation** affects navigation safety, sensor performance, and GPS-timing-dependent systems; alternate-navigation fits and procedures are uneven across the force (FFIR-4). Protecting dispersed seabed infrastructure with limited hulls is infeasible everywhere at once, forcing dependency-based prioritization. Polar-night and icing degrade lookout, aviation, and small-boat operations.
- **Running risk.** HIGH (driven by PNT). Mitigated by alternate-navigation activation (DP-5), EMCON discipline, layered repair-ship protection, and dependency-prioritized CUI coverage.

- **PNT-degraded navigation:** The polar-night, high-latitude environment already stresses navigation (poor celestial reference, high-latitude compass error); layered onto the **GPS/PNT jamming and AIS spoofing** over Finnmark and the Svalbard approaches, this makes precise station-keeping over a cut site, corridor patrol, and de-confliction of friendly surface and air tracks materially harder, and elevates the value of alternate-navigation and counter-EW measures. The EMS and PNT picture, and the SPACECOM coordination seam, are developed in `11_Annexes.md` (Cyber/EW and Climatology annexes) and the running estimates (`14_Running_Estimates.md`).

- **GPS/PNT jamming picture.** Sustained Kola-based GPS/PNT jamming and AIS spoofing degrade navigation across Finnmark and the Svalbard approaches, peaking 11 JAN coincident with the Nordkapp Data Link faults. Source is assessed as Northern Fleet EW units on the Kola Peninsula (Tobol-/Murmansk-BN-analog). The footprint affects friendly, civil, and adversary receivers alike; full characterization of extent, pattern, and effect is a collection priority (PIR-4).

## 3. Character of the offensive

The consolidation is led by Iranian-backed proxy militias — principally Liwa al-Sadiq, reinforced, with elements of Saraya Khorasan — operating alongside but distinct from Syrian regime regular formations. The proxy character of the lead echelon is assessed with moderate confidence and resolves only by cross-reading signals and human reporting against the adversary order of battle (document 03); surface and open-source reporting attribute the action to regime regulars. The Ansar Advisory Group is assessed to provide command, enabling, and indirect-fire coordination; its hand is concealed to preserve Iranian deniability. Employment of proxies in the lead is assessed as a deliberate measure to keep Iranian direction below the threshold of attributable state action.

## 4. Partner force — Azadî Resistance Council

The ARC is a Kurdish-led umbrella movement with Arab tribal affiliates of variable reliability. It is organized consistent with a doctrinal resistance:

- **Underground (Komel network).** Clandestine cells in the urban centers of Hasakah and Qamishli conducting intelligence, subversion, and early warning. Assessed penetrated by regime intelligence; communications security weak.

- **Auxiliary (Hêlîn network).** A clandestine support element providing logistics, safe houses, movement assistance, and early warning to the guerrilla force.

- **Guerrilla force (Roj Brigades).** The overt military arm, an estimated 2,500 fighters with limited heavy weapons, low ammunition stocks, and no organic sustainment independent of route BADGER.

Partner cohesion is assessed as adequate at present but degrading. Absent restoration of resupply, the Roj Brigades are assessed at risk of culmination or fragmentation within the near term — the binding planning timeline for any external support.

## 3. Lines of communication

**Route BADGER (severed).** Principal external support corridor for the Tel Roj pocket: from the Iraqi border vicinity the Rabia/Yaroubiya crossing, southwest along secondary roads to the Tel Roj junction, into the pocket. Interdicted at the Tel Roj junction by Iranian-backed proxy action on 150600Z MAR 2026. The junction is the binding chokepoint; while held by hostile forces, the corridor is closed to sustained movement. Shortest route; lowest sustainment leg; highest fixed-chokepoint interdiction risk.

**Route SABER (alternate).** Longer alternate offsetting south through the desert margin from the al-Walid–al-Tanf area crossing, avoiding the Tel Roj junction but crossing open terrain under potential observation and within range of proxy indirect fire. Trades a fixed-chokepoint interdiction risk for exposure across distance and a longer, more lift-intensive sustainment leg.

## 5. Sustainment geography

Sustainment of a force in the pocket must traverse distance from the Iraqi border under interdiction threat; throughput is capped by corridor capacity and by available lift, not by stockholding at the point of origin. The absence of northern access (Turkish opposition) removes the shortest potential line of support and forces reliance on the longer eastern and southeastern approaches. Aerial resupply and recovery transit Russian air-defense coverage and require deconfliction.

## 5. Population and terrain

The Jazira and the middle Euphrates valley present an ethnic-mosaic human terrain of Kurdish, Arab tribal, and minority communities. Partner legitimacy and freedom of movement vary by district: strong in Kurdish-majority districts of Hasakah and Qamishli, contested in Arab-majority districts along the Euphrates, where the ARC is viewed with suspicion and the population is more susceptible to regime and proxy influence. Internally displaced concentrations in Hasakah governorate add civil density and complicate the distinction between combatants and non-combatants.

## 6. Electronic and information environment

Adversary electronic warfare — attributed to proxy and Iranian-advisory systems and to Russian-enabled capability resident in theater — degrades Global Positioning System reception and tactical communications across the Euphrates valley. The information environment is contested by regime, Iranian, and Russian narratives, including a pre-emptive attribution narrative directed at United States and partner activity.

**Situation.** Command of the line of effort runs USCENTCOM–SOCCENT–SOTF-L; the partner is supported, not commanded. Adversary electronic warfare degrades tactical communications and position, navigation, and timing across the valley. **Capability / shortfall.** A combined Azadî Resistance Council–SOTF-L architecture must be established and hardened against jamming; low-probability-of-intercept and alternate-navigation means are required. Partner communications security is weak. **Estimate.** Command and control is feasible but dependent on a resilient, low-signature architecture and on the by-with-through relationship being clearly framed. C2 resilience is a dependency, not a given.

National strategy identifies the countering of Iranian malign influence across the region as an enduring objective, with specific reference to denying Iran a contiguous ground line of communication ("land bridge") from Iranian territory through Iraq and Syria toward the Mediterranean littoral. National strategy directs the prevention of the reconstitution of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) and the protection of gains achieved against it. National strategy emphasizes the use of partners and economy-of-force approaches, and the avoidance of large-scale, open-ended United States ground commitments.

## 2. National Defense Strategy (relevant direction)

Department strategy directs the imposition of cost on Iranian-backed consolidation in eastern Syria through partnered and irregular approaches, **without escalation to overt armed conflict** with the Syrian regime or with Iran. Department strategy designates the eastern Syria effort as a supporting effort within the broader theater campaign, to be resourced accordingly, and directs that the introduction of United States forces into ground combat in Syria is **not authorized** under this line of effort.

## 3. National Military Strategy / CJCS direction (relevant direction)

Military strategy directs combatant commands to develop options that achieve campaign objectives below the threshold of armed conflict, with explicit attention to authorities, attribution management, and escalation control. Support to vetted irregular forces conducting authorized unconventional warfare is to be conducted under Section 1202 (FY2018 National Defense Authorization Act); activities exceeding that authority are to be referred for separate authorization. All support to partner forces is conditioned on completion of human-rights (Leahy) vetting.

## 4. Theater strategy and commander's strategic estimate (excerpts)

The USCENTCOM theater strategy assesses the loss of partner-held terrain in the middle Euphrates valley as a reversal of counter-ISIS gains and as an enabler of Iranian land-bridge consolidation. The commander's strategic estimate assesses that an indigenous resistance — the Azadî Resistance Council (ARC) — retains latent capability in the Jazira but has been displaced and isolated from external resupply by recent Iranian-backed proxy action.

The theater strategy sets the desired conditions as: a viable indigenous capability able to coerce and disrupt regime and Iranian-backed proxy activity in the Jazira; a stalled consolidation in the middle Euphrates valley; and a minimized United States advisory footprint maintained below the threshold of overt armed conflict. The estimate notes that apportioned forces for the eastern Syria supporting effort are limited, that intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance and lift are shared theater assets prioritized against higher-priority requirements elsewhere in the area of responsibility, and that force closure for this line of effort is therefore time-phased and lift-dependent.

## 7. Residual ISIS threat

ISIS remnant cells persist in the Badia desert and exploit security vacuums. Diversion of regime and proxy attention toward a resistance buildup is assessed as a condition that could enable localized ISIS resurgence, with attendant risk to lines of communication and to the broader counter-ISIS gains the campaign seeks to protect.

- **Intelligence.** Make priority requirements of partner reliability and penetration, adversary intent and the proxy reinforcement timeline, and corridor trafficability; treat ISIS resurgence as a monitored named area of interest; do not assume persistent intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance coverage.

## Disaster situation

Severe Tropical Cyclone RUA struck Efate at 050600Z FEB 2026 as a Category-5 system and tracked across the central islands. Initial reporting indicates severe damage to Port Vila, including to the Bauerfield International Airport airfield surfaces and terminal and to the Lapetasi (Port Vila) wharf. Power, water, and fixed communications across Efate are largely inoperative. Casualty and displacement figures are incomplete; displacement is reported across Efate, the Shepherd Islands, and parts of Espiritu Santo, with the most acute needs assessed in water, emergency medical care, and shelter.

The Republic of Vanuatu is a Y-shaped archipelago of some eighty islands in the Southwest Pacific. The population is concentrated on Efate (capital, Port Vila) and Espiritu Santo (Luganville), with substantial dispersed populations across the Shepherd Islands and the northern and southern island groups. The terrain is volcanic and mountainous, the population is largely coastal, and many communities are reachable only by sea or air.

## Air points of entry

- **Bauerfield International Airport (Port Vila, Efate).** The principal international airport. Cyclone damage to airfield surfaces, navigational aids, and the terminal has reduced throughput; ramp space and materials-handling equipment are limited even when the field is usable. Restoration of throughput is a precondition for sustained fixed-wing relief into the capital.

- **Santo-Pekoa International Airport (Luganville, Espiritu Santo).** A secondary field, less affected, offering an alternate aerial entry point for the north.

## Sea points of entry

- **Lapetasi (Port Vila) wharf, Efate.** The principal commercial wharf, partially blocked and structurally degraded by the cyclone; berthing for relief shipping is constrained pending survey and clearance.

- **Luganville (Simon Peter) wharf, Espiritu Santo.** A large, modern, Chinese-built wharf, intact, capable of berthing large vessels. It is both a logistics opportunity and a point of competition, given its provenance and the competitor's interest.

- **Over-the-shore and sea-basing.** Given degraded fixed ports, delivery by landing craft, connectors, and air from sea-based shipping is a feasible alternative that reduces dependence on contested fixed infrastructure and on a single point of host-nation approval.

## Internal distribution

The dispersed, multi-island population means that arrival of relief at a port of entry does not equate to delivery; distribution to the Shepherd Islands and other outer groups requires rotary-wing and small-craft movement and is the harder half of the throughput problem. Customary authority and damaged local infrastructure further shape distribution.

## J4 — Logistics

Logistics is the binding factor. The problem is throughput over distance, not stockholding: relief must be moved across thousands of nautical miles and then distributed among dispersed islands. Degraded ports at Port Vila constrain fixed-port throughput; the intact Luganville wharf and sea-basing are the principal alternatives. Lift and sealift are shared, time-phased assets; closure of the full force is measured in weeks, while the most acute needs are measured in days.

Vanuatu governance is in a period of instability associated with a motion-of-no-confidence cycle. A parliamentary grouping favorable to the People's Republic of China — referred to in open reporting as the Vanua Tasi bloc — is maneuvering for advantage and is assessed to favor channeling international assistance through People's Republic of China auspices. Reporting indicates that access for United States and allied responders to Port Vila and to certain affected districts has been subject to restriction; whether this reflects a deliberate, directed policy or administrative confusion in the disaster's aftermath is not confirmed and is assessed at moderate confidence to be at least partly deliberate.

Vanuatu is a parliamentary republic. Governments are typically multi-party coalitions, and motions of no confidence are a frequent feature of political life. At the time of the cyclone, a motion-of-no-confidence cycle is in progress and no faction holds a settled majority. A parliamentary grouping referred to as the Vanua Tasi bloc favors closer alignment with the People's Republic of China and is influential in the current maneuvering; a caretaker leadership exercises authority pending resolution. The practical consequence for foreign responders is that the locus of host-nation consent is uncertain: requests and clearances routed through one set of officials may be countermanded or delayed by another.

## Foreign relations

Vanuatu maintains relationships with Australia, New Zealand, France, and the United States, and has accepted infrastructure investment and policing cooperation from the People's Republic of China. Vanuatu has a record of balancing external partners to preserve its own freedom of action, including declining arrangements perceived to constrain assistance from third parties.

## Society and humanitarian context

Vanuatu is among the most disaster-exposed states in the world and has prior experience hosting large international relief operations following major cyclones. Customary authority (chiefs) is significant at the community level, particularly on outer islands, and affects how relief is received and distributed. The United Nations humanitarian system, through the cluster mechanism, and a range of non-governmental organizations are established partners in Vanuatu disaster response.

The Republic of Vanuatu is a Y-shaped archipelago of some eighty islands in the Southwest Pacific. The population is concentrated on Efate (capital, Port Vila) and Espiritu Santo (Luganville), with substantial dispersed populations across the Shepherd Islands and the northern and southern island groups. The terrain is volcanic and mountainous, the population is largely coastal, and many communities are reachable only by sea or air.

## Government and politics

Vanuatu is a parliamentary republic. Governments are typically multi-party coalitions, and motions of no confidence are a frequent feature of political life. At the time of the cyclone, a motion-of-no-confidence cycle is in progress and no faction holds a settled majority. A parliamentary grouping referred to as the Vanua Tasi bloc favors closer alignment with the People's Republic of China and is influential in the current maneuvering; a caretaker leadership exercises authority pending resolution. The practical consequence for foreign responders is that the locus of host-nation consent is uncertain: requests and clearances routed through one set of officials may be countermanded or delayed by another.

## Foreign relations

Vanuatu maintains relationships with Australia, New Zealand, France, and the United States, and has accepted infrastructure investment and policing cooperation from the People's Republic of China. Vanuatu has a record of balancing external partners to preserve its own freedom of action, including declining arrangements perceived to constrain assistance from third parties.

## Society and humanitarian context

Severe Tropical Cyclone RUA struck Efate at 050600Z FEB 2026 as a Category-5 system and tracked across the central islands. Initial reporting indicates severe damage to Port Vila, including to the Bauerfield International Airport airfield surfaces and terminal and to the Lapetasi (Port Vila) wharf. Power, water, and fixed communications across Efate are largely inoperative. Casualty and displacement figures are incomplete; displacement is reported across Efate, the Shepherd Islands, and parts of Espiritu Santo, with the most acute needs assessed in water, emergency medical care, and shelter.

## Political situation

Vanuatu governance is in a period of instability associated with a motion-of-no-confidence cycle. A parliamentary grouping favorable to the People's Republic of China — referred to in open reporting as the Vanua Tasi bloc — is maneuvering for advantage and is assessed to favor channeling international assistance through People's Republic of China auspices. Reporting indicates that access for United States and allied responders to Port Vila and to certain affected districts has been subject to restriction; whether this reflects a deliberate, directed policy or administrative confusion in the disaster's aftermath is not confirmed and is assessed at moderate confidence to be at least partly deliberate.

## Competitor presence

A People's Republic of China relief flotilla, including the People's Liberation Army Navy hospital ship and surface escorts and a China Coast Guard cutter, is operating in Vanuatu waters. People's Republic of China police advisors associated with the standing policing-cooperation arrangement are reported ashore. People's Republic of China messaging emphasizes the speed and generosity of its assistance and characterizes a United States military role as militarized and potentially destabilizing.

## Infrastructure and access

Outer-island populations are difficult to reach and are assessed to be underserved by the relief that has so far arrived.

The People's Republic of China presence comprises a naval hospital ship and escorts, a coast-guard cutter, police advisors ashore, and infrastructure leverage (the Luganville wharf). People's Republic of China activity is gray-zone and below the threshold of armed conflict; force is assessed unlikely, while shadowing, visibility competition, and exploitation of United States or allied missteps are likely. The surface presentation of the presence as humanitarian is distinguished from its assessed strategic-access purpose. Regime-style penetration is not the issue here; the competitor's strength is narrative and presence, and its vulnerability is the perception of self-interest and coercion.

## Step 4 — Determine threat/competitor courses of action and analytic gaps

The most likely competitor course of action is to maintain a visible, "benevolent" relief presence, deepen access through a sympathetic host-nation bloc, and avoid any incident that would justify a firm United States or allied response. A course of action of concern is the use of the host-nation bloc to restrict United States and allied access while the People's Republic of China fills the resulting gap. Key gaps the staff must resolve through information requirements include the true locus and stability of host-nation consent, People's Republic of China intent and likely response to a United States and allied effort, the throughput and restoration timeline of the ports of entry, and the location and needs of dispersed populations. - Coordinated messaging portrays People's Republic of China assistance as fast, generous, and respectful of Vanuatu sovereignty, and portrays a United States military role as militarized and escalatory.

- Messaging amplifies any United States or allied action that can be characterized as infringing Vanuatu sovereignty or as slow and conditional.

## Assessed intent (moderate confidence)

The People's Republic of China seeks to be seen as the indispensable relief provider, to deepen durable access and influence under humanitarian cover, and to keep its activity ambiguous and below any threshold that would justify a firm United States or allied response. People's Republic of China forces are assessed unlikely to physically obstruct United States or allied relief by force, but are likely to shadow, to compete for visibility, and to exploit any United States misstep.
- \(3\) Deconflict operations with co-located People's Republic of China forces and avoid any armed incident.

The most likely competitor course of action is to maintain a visible, "benevolent" relief presence, deepen access through a sympathetic host-nation bloc, and avoid any incident that would justify a firm United States or allied response. A course of action of concern is the use of the host-nation bloc to restrict United States and allied access while the People's Republic of China fills the resulting gap. Key gaps the staff must resolve through information requirements include the true locus and stability of host-nation consent, People's Republic of China intent and likely response to a United States and allied effort, the throughput and restoration timeline of the ports of entry, and the location and needs of dispersed populations. This brief does not nominate information requirements, decision points, or courses of action for the friendly force; those are products of the mission analysis.

When directed, USINDOPACOM conducts foreign humanitarian assistance and disaster relief in the Republic of Vanuatu by, with, and through the FRANZ partners, in order to relieve human suffering and support the affected state, while remaining below the threshold of armed conflict.

## 3. Execution

a\. **Commander's intent (higher).** The purpose is to deliver timely, credible United States relief in support of the civilian-led response and to reinforce the sovereignty and resilience of the affected state and the standing of its partners. The method is supporting, enabling, and coordinated action that places civilian and host-nation authorities forward and the United States military in support. The desired end state is an affected population stabilized, relief transitioned to civilian, United Nations, and host-nation authorities, and partner access and legitimacy preserved, with United States involvement held below the threshold of armed conflict.

France, Australia, and New Zealand coordinate disaster response in the region through the FRANZ Arrangement, and each maintains standing relationships with Vanuatu. A United States contribution is expected to reinforce, not supplant, this regional architecture; a response that places Pacific and FRANZ partners forward carries greater legitimacy than a unilateral United States effort.

## Strategic guidance bearing on the operation

The intent at the national level is to relieve suffering, to reinforce the sovereignty and resilience of the affected state and the standing of its partners, and to deny the consolidation of competitor access — while keeping United States involvement below the threshold of armed conflict. Speed and legitimacy are to be pursued together. A response that is slow cedes the competition; a response that is heavy-handed or that proceeds without the affected state's consent undermines the very legitimacy it seeks to protect.

The relief effort is to be fast, visibly cooperative with the affected state and the FRANZ partners, and disciplined in keeping the United States military in a support and assist role. Speed and legitimacy are to be weighed together; neither a slow response nor an overbearing one serves the end state. The command's standing is best protected by enabling others and by being seen to respect Vanuatu sovereignty.

1.  Feasibility of relief delivery given degraded ports and the distances involved.

2.  Host-nation consent and legitimacy, and the civilian (USAID) and host-nation lead.

3.  Coordination and integration with the FRANZ partners and the United Nations humanitarian system.

4.  Escalation management and deconfliction with co-located competitor forces.

5.  Force protection and the preservation of humanitarian neutrality.

(See PACOM TCP JIPOE) China currently occupies the islands of Quemoy and Matsu, having seized them without provocation on June 10 and June 18 respectively. \(E\) Commander's Initial Analysis. This is a crisis-action problem in which time is the dominant factor: civilians are being killed ashore and along the coast now, people are drowning at sea now, and the flow is expected to grow, so credible interception, rescue, and no-fly-zone enforcement capacity must be on station at once. Several features will shape every option. First, this is a Maritime Interception Operation with an air-protection mission layered onto it, and the Navy leads it. We interdict, that is, deny passage to, the arms and oil the blockade forbids; we intercept, that is, detect, board, search, and take from the water, the people attempting the crossing; and we now also enforce a no-fly zone to stop the killing of civilians from the air. Those are distinct tasks and I want them spoken of with precision. The Coast Guard is integral to the interception and to the handling of those we bring aboard, and the Department of Homeland Security remains the lead for their immigration disposition; but the operation itself is a Navy-led military operation, not a law-enforcement action, and I do not intend to conduct the maritime piece inside United States waters, where it would become one. Second, a word on terms. I will refer to those we take from the water as migrants. That is a deliberate choice: the label keeps their disposition a matter of policy and does not, of itself, confer a legal status we are in no position to adjudicate from the deck of a cutter. Planners should nonetheless understand that many are in fact refugees fleeing violence, that the longer they remain displaced the more that status will assert itself, and that the distinction bears directly on where and how they may lawfully be sent; treat it as a matter for analysis. Third, the President has already used force in declaring the no-fly zone and warning that further killings will be met forcefully, and I read my authority accordingly: I am authorized now to enforce the no-fly zone and to use force to stop atrocities in progress, including engaging drones or coastal craft caught in the act of attacking civilians. That is deliberate, limited force to protect non-combatants; it is not a general war with Cuba, and it is not license for the graver steps. Fourth, feasibility will turn less on combat power than on throughput: whether the combined interception, rescue, and reception capacity, afloat, at the Guantanamo Migrant Operations Center, and at partner facilities under United Nations supervision, can keep pace with the flow. No one we take from the water will be returned to Cuba; on that point I want no ambiguity, and the customary prohibition on returning people to persecution is therefore honored as a matter of policy. The planning problem is not whether to repatriate but where to process and shelter those we intercept, and what that requires of us. Disposition begins outside the continental United States, at Guantanamo Bay and in Puerto Rico, and I am treating the establishment of that reception and processing capacity as a requirement, because it will define our basing, our lift, and our sustainment. Whether we then move Cubans onward to processing sites in the continental United States, as was done during the Mariel influx, is a national decision with sharp domestic political consequences in both directions, and I want it framed as a decision, not pre-empted. Fifth, we are acting without a Security Council mandate, over a Russian and Chinese veto, and against an adversary information campaign that calls our evidence a pretext for invasion; the legitimacy of the civilian-protection case is therefore a center of gravity in its own right, and nothing we do should hand Havana, Moscow, or Beijing the invasion narrative they are seeking. Sixth, and gravest, the hardest decision this crisis may force on me is ashore: whether to put forces on Cuban soil to protect civilians or as the leading edge of the regime-change option I have been directed to prepare. That decision carries the full weight of sovereignty and national commitment; I want mission analysis to frame it honestly, to identify the indicators and decision points that would bring it before me, and to keep it distinct, in fact and in perception, from the operation we begin now. Guantanamo Bay must be treated as both a place of safety and an installation under threat.

\(E\) The President sought a United Nations Security Council resolution authorizing a United Nations-led force to protect Cuban civilians. The Russian Federation and the People's Republic of China vetoed it, and both now describe the atrocity reporting as imperialist propaganda intended to manufacture a pretext for invasion. Acting without a Security Council mandate, the President declared a no-fly zone over the Cuban coast and stated that any further killings would be dealt with forcefully. The United States thus acts on a civilian-protection rationale under customary international law, over the objection of two great powers, and the legitimacy of that case is now itself a strategic center of gravity.

**5. (E) UNITED STATES INTERESTS AND AIMS.**

\(E\) The United States seeks to stop the killing of Cuban civilians, to prevent further loss of life at sea, to enforce the no-fly zone and the blockade, to avoid a wider armed conflict with the Cuban state, to sustain the legitimacy of the civilian-protection effort against the adversary narrative, and to preserve for national decision the graver options of acting ashore, whether to protect civilians directly or to enable a change of regime.

**6. (E) THE DISPOSITION PROBLEM AND ITS POLITICS.**

\(E\) What becomes of those taken from the water is a strategic question in its own right. No one will be returned to Cuba. Processing will begin outside the continental United States, at Guantanamo Bay and in Puerto Rico, and the question of whether to bring Cubans onward to processing sites in the continental United States, as was done during the Mariel influx, is a national decision that divides domestic opinion sharply in both directions: bringing them ashore would satisfy the Cuban American community and much moderate opinion while drawing strong opposition from constituencies favoring immigration restriction, and declining to do so would reverse those reactions. The commander must plan for the reception and processing that either course requires while leaving the decision itself to national authority.

**7. (E) THE SHADOW OF THE GRAVER OPTIONS.**

\(E\) The direction to prepare, on order, plans for operations ashore and for regime change hangs over the whole effort. The decision to commit forces ashore is the decisive decision for which indicators and decision points are being developed.**

**6. (E) J6 COMMUNICATIONS. Command and control for a dispersed maritime and air operation, coalition and interagency interoperability, and assured communications with the reception sites are being established. The information environment requires a robust capability to document and rapidly release evidence in support of the legitimacy of the civilian-protection case.**

**7. (E) SURGEON / MEDICAL. Mass at-sea rescue of people from unseaworthy craft in the Florida Current will generate a mass-casualty and public-health demand: hypothermia, near-drowning, dehydration, and the care of vulnerable populations. Afloat medical aboard the amphibious force, and medical capacity at Guantanamo Bay and Puerto Rico, are limiting factors being sized against projected flow.**

\(E\) Proposed Termination Criteria. Evaluate and recommend modification: the killing of civilians stopped and the no-fly zone uncontested; preventable deaths at sea halted; the flow managed to a sustainable level; intercepted migrants safe and lawfully processed outside the continental United States and, as nationally decided, onward, with none returned to Cuba; no wider armed conflict with the Cuban state and Guantanamo Bay secure; and the options ashore developed and preserved without commitment. Translate these into measurable, observable criteria in the Commander's Estimate.

\(E\) Proposed Post-Crisis Considerations. Evaluate the transition of the effort to the Department of Homeland Security and the interagency for durable disposition, to include onward movement to the continental United States and resettlement; the sustainment of partner and United Nations arrangements; the protracted-displacement problem of Cubans who cannot go home until conditions change; and the enduring information and legitimacy contest.

\(E\) The Department of Homeland Security and the United States Coast Guard are supported for the disposition of migrants; the military supports that line of effort.

\(E\) United States Transportation Command (lift and sustainment of reception basing), United States Northern Command (homeland interface and any onward movement to the continental United States), United States Special Operations Command and United States Space Command (compartmented branches; intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and space support), the Department of State (diplomacy, third-country processing, United Nations arrangements), and the Department of Justice (law-enforcement contingencies) are supporting.

**7. (E) INTERAGENCY. The Department of Homeland Security and the United States Coast Guard lead migrant disposition; the Department of State leads diplomacy, third-country processing, and United Nations coordination; the Department of Justice supports law-enforcement contingencies. Reception and processing are to be established outside the continental United States, at Guantanamo Bay and in Puerto Rico.**

**Method.** I intend to rapidly close coalition forces into the Indo-Pacific; establish sea control and air superiority in the JOA through coalition operations; isolate and degrade the PRC militarized Spratly outposts as the operational center of gravity; restore Philippine sovereignty at Pag-asa through controlled amphibious operations that minimize civilian casualties; and create the diplomatic conditions for PRC acceptance of an off-ramp. ### 4.1 Seasonal Pattern

**Late Wet Season (Late August — Operations Window):**

- **Monsoon:** Southwest monsoon (until ~early October).

- **Prevailing winds:** Southwest at 15–25 knots; gusts higher in convective weather; wind shifts during typhoon transit.

- **Sea state:** 3–4 typical; can rise to 5–6 in convective or typhoon conditions.

- **Visibility:** 6–10 nm typical; reduced in afternoon thunderstorms (1–3 nm).

- **Precipitation:** Heavy convective rainfall, particularly afternoon / evening; cumulative monsoon rainfall 200–400 mm/month.

### 4.2 Tropical Cyclones (Typhoons)

- **Peak season:** August through October. Pag-asa cluster is in the typhoon track region.

- **Genesis:** Western North Pacific east of the Philippines; tracks generally west / west-northwest.

- **Frequency:** ~25 named storms per year globally; ~7–9 reach Spratly/Philippine area annually.

- **Speed:** Typically 10–15 knots forward; can intensify rapidly under favorable SST.

- **Implications:** May force pause in amphibious / air operations; force-protection posture changes; SAR demand increases.

- **Forecast horizon:** 5–7 days reliable; PACOM Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC) at Pearl Harbor provides theater forecasts.

- **Air operations:** F-35B / MV-22 LHA operations remain feasible to sea state 5; degraded above.

- **Submarine operations:** Generally insensitive to surface conditions.

**Acceptable Risk.** I accept moderate risk to force in the conduct of sea control and air superiority operations against PRC A2/AD; I accept moderate risk to mission timeline in trade for civilian casualty avoidance; I do not accept risk of strategic escalation (PRC mainland targeting, nuclear posture changes, Taiwan Strait war).

**Enemy threats.** PRC ASCM (sea / sub / air / land-based); PRC SAM (HQ-9B from outposts; long-range from mainland); PRC theater-range fires (PLARF DF-26B / DF-21D); PRC cyber (VOLT / SALT TYPHOON); PRC counter-space; PRC information operations / disinformation; PRC submarine forces. PRC has demonstrated willingness for asymmetric / deniable action.

**Friendly protection posture.** FPCON BRAVO theater-wide; FPCON CHARLIE at forward sites. Aegis BMD-capable Type 052D and 7th Fleet equivalents at sea; ground-based PATRIOT and THAAD coverage where positioned. FLTCYBERCOM CPTs (2) for DCO. SOCPAC PR capability. USSPACECOM space-domain awareness.

**Civilian considerations.** Substantial Philippine, US, and TCN civilians at risk; commercial traffic exposed; submarine cable users (telecommunications providers; internet routing) affected.

**Assumptions.** - PRC will not initiate strategic-escalation kinetic action against US forces (per MLCOA). - PRC cyber action will be persistent but at threshold below war-crime severity. - Submarine cable interdiction is a credible PRC option not yet activated. - Coalition force-protection cooperation will continue.

### 5.2 Mission (Protection)

Protect coalition forces, partner forces, critical infrastructure (C2, ISR, SPOD/APOD, submarine cables), and Philippine civilian populations against adversary threats across all domains; conduct effective Personnel Recovery; manage POW / detainee processes under international law.

### 5.3 Analysis

**Capabilities.** - Aegis BMD; PATRIOT; THAAD; integrated air and missile defense network. - Submarine awareness via P-8A, T-AGOS, SSN-on-SSN tracking. - Cyber defensive operations through FLTCYBERCOM CPTs and USCYBERCOM backstop. - Coalition force-protection cooperation (allied AAW destroyers add SM-6 capacity). - Personnel Recovery capability via SOCPAC, 129 RQS HH-60G.

**Limitations.** - DF-26B / DF-21D coverage from PLA Rocket Force at theater range; only Aegis BMD or specialized SSC capability defends. - PRC counter-space and PNT-denial may degrade BMD radar coverage. - Submarine cable protection is inherently limited — cables are vulnerable and prevention is hard. - Coalition CENTRIXS provisioning lag may delay full IAMD interoperability. - POW handling capacity in theater is modest; ICRC engagement critical.

**Critical Issues.** - AFP/PCG personnel detained at Pag-asa (~25 captured) require ICRC engagement and care for POW protection. - US citizens believed captured at Pag-asa (3 contractors) require diplomatic and ICRC engagement. - Pag-asa civilian population (~250) is at risk in any kinetic restoration; evacuation planning critical. - Cable disruption risk requires industry coordination and rapid-repair capability. - Force-protection at SPOD / APOD nodes (high-density US presence) is a force-protection challenge.

**Risks.** - HIGH: Detained personnel mistreatment (mitigated by ICRC engagement and PRC accountability statements). - MED-HIGH: Successful PRC ASCM engagement of US/coalition surface combatant. - MED: Pag-asa civilian casualties during restoration. - MED: Submarine cable disruption. - MED: Cyber action against critical infrastructure (financial, energy, transportation). - LOW: PRC PLARF kinetic action against forward bases.

**Assumptions.** - Coalition partners will complete national authorization for OPCON transfer NLT N+10. - SATCOM bandwidth augmentation will be granted within 5 days of RFF. - PRC cyber and EW activity against C2 will be persistent but manageable through DCO.

### 1.2 Mission (C2)

Establish and maintain a coherent, resilient, redundant Command and Control architecture that enables COMJTF-PACIFIC HARRIER to direct joint and coalition operations across the JOA under contested conditions, with assured connectivity to CDR USINDOPACOM, subordinate components, coalition partners, and Philippine forces.

### 1.3 Analysis

**Capabilities.** - Forward-deployed C2 platform (USS *Blue Ridge* LCC-19) provides afloat C2 for maritime operations. - AOC at Hickam provides air-component C2. - BCC at WESCOM provides bilateral PH-US coordination. - FLTCYBERCOM CPTs (2) provide defensive cyber. - Multiple coalition LNO cells planned.

**Limitations.** - SATCOM bandwidth constraint may force prioritization decisions during contested phases. - PNT denial / spoofing in JOA expected; will affect time-synchronized C2 (Link 16, JREAP-C). - Japanese forces national-command retention limits integrated operations. - Coalition CENTRIXS classification management is a friction point.

**Critical Issues.** - C2 standup timeline (JTF HQ at Camp H.M. Smith) — current best estimate N+3 for initial operating capability, N+10 for full operating capability. Tight against planning timeline. - Allied LNO cell integration — particularly RAAF / RAF / JMSDF — requires CENTRIXS / coalition-network access provisioning that historically takes 7–14 days. - BCC architecture is a precedent-setting structure under existing MDB/SEB — agreements may require minor revision; coordinating with EMB Manila.

**Risks.** - HIGH: SATCOM bandwidth saturation under sustained operations. - MED: PNT denial degrading time-synchronized C2. - MED: Coalition CENTRIXS provisioning timeline slipping past N+10. - LOW: PRC cyber action denying primary C2 paths (mitigated by PACE).

### 1.4 Conclusions and Recommendations

JTF C2 architecture is achievable on planning timeline with the following actions:

1.  **Immediate (NLT N+1):** Submit RFF to USSPACECOM for additional SATCOM bandwidth (40% augmentation requested).

2.  **Immediate (NLT N+1):** Initiate CENTRIXS provisioning for AU / UK / JP / NZ LNO cells; expedite through partner liaison.

3.  **NLT N+3:** Stand up JTF HQ at Camp H.M. Smith; activate BCC at WESCOM.

4.  **NLT N+5:** Coalition LNO cells operational at JTF HQ.

5.  **NLT N+10:** JTF HQ full operating capability; redundant C2 paths exercised.

(4) (E) EXERCISE OPCON OF ALLOCATED FORCES UPON TOA.\
(5) (E) ACCEPT TACON / OPCON OF COALITION FORCES UPON NATIONAL TRANSFER OF AUTHORITY AS REFLECTED IN REF F PARA 20.\

### 2.4 Strategic Priorities — Southeast Asia and ASEAN

The United States continues to support an ASEAN-centered regional architecture but recognizes that ASEAN consensus mechanisms have been repeatedly fractured by PRC influence on individual member states. Vietnam, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Singapore are the primary US partners on SCS and SLOC issues; Cambodia and Laos have aligned more closely with PRC positions.

### 6.1 Political (P)

- **Philippines.** Marcos Administration unified; emergency NSC sessions ongoing; AFP Chief of Staff and PCG Commandant in active coordination with US counterparts. Domestic Filipino public sentiment is unified in support of restoration; political risk to the alliance from a *limited* US response is high.

- **PRC.** CCP / CMC firmly committed to Pag-asa retention as a face-saving and strategic-narrative imperative. Domestic PRC population mobilized through state media around “Tiexian defense”; reversal would be politically costly for the regime.

- **ASEAN.** Indonesia, Vietnam, Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei aligned in private with US-Philippines position; Cambodia and Laos non-aligned. ASEAN consensus statement on attribution remains stalled; bilateral support is the active mechanism.

### 3.6 Singapore (Major Security Cooperation Partner)

**Posture:** - Sembawang Naval Base / Changi Naval Base port access for US and coalition vessels. - Paya Lebar / Tengah air base access for tankers and ISR. - KC-30 (RSAF) tanker support upon Singaporean Government authorization (expected).

### 3.7 Vietnam (Comprehensive Strategic Partner)

**Posture (quiet — not in WARNORD):** - Intelligence sharing on Vanguard Bank / Spratly area. - Overflight clearance over Vietnamese territorial airspace for P-8A / P-1. - Cam Ranh Bay logistics access (limited; not for combatant flagging). - No public alignment.

### 3.8 Indonesia (Comprehensive Strategic Partner)

**Posture (quiet — not in WARNORD):** - TNI-AL / Bakamla coordination on Natuna and Sulu Sea SLOC patrols. - Lombok / Sunda strait transit clearance. - No public alignment; no force contribution.

### 3.9 Malaysia (Strategic Partner)

**Posture (quiet — not in WARNORD):** - Kota Kinabalu port access (limited). - RMAF Labuan air base access (limited; not for combatant operations). - Intelligence sharing on Luconia Shoals. - No public alignment.

### 3.10 Brunei (FPDA-adjacent)

**Posture:** - Bandar Seri Begawan support. - Royal Brunei Armed Forces sustainment access.

### 7.2 Mission (Information)

Through coordinated narrative alignment, counter-information operations, electronic warfare, and cyberspace operations, support CDR USINDOPACOM’s strategic objectives by: (a) maintaining factual coalition narrative dominance in English-language and partner-language spaces; (b) countering PRC “lawful enforcement” framing; (c) demonstrating coalition unity; (d) enabling kinetic action through information effects (deception, denial); (e) preserving operational security.

### 7.3 Analysis

**Capabilities.** - Coordinated coalition strategic communications. - Philippine AFP / PCG Transparency Initiative as factual rebuttal mechanism. - CSIS AMTI and partner think-tank network as third-party validators. - Cyberspace defensive capability (FLTCYBERCOM CPTs). - Electronic warfare capability (USAF E-EC; USN E-18G; USMC EA-6B / E-EC; allied EW units).

**Limitations.** - PRC narrative dominance in Mandarin-language space is structural. - AI-generated content detection is imperfect; disinformation prevalence will be high. - Coalition strategic-communications coordination has friction (different national agendas). - Offensive cyber against PRC infrastructure outside JOA requires Presidential release. - EW operations against PRC mainland sensors require Presidential release.

**Critical Issues.** - “Lawful enforcement” framing — needs continuous factual rebuttal grounded in PCA Award / UNCLOS. - Civilian-casualty narrative — every strike must be defensible; OPLAW review with IO coordination. - Coalition cohesion narrative — visible coalition unity matters more than messaging volume. - Counter-disinformation rapid-response — particularly against AI-generated content depicting purported AFP atrocities. - Operational security — protecting coalition force-flow patterns from PRC ISR / OSINT-collection.

Total channel distance Daru to Kiunga is 510 river miles. Loaded upriver transit is four to five days; downriver three. The channel is unmarked above Obo and is navigated by local knowledge; the Ok Tedi river operation maintains its own pilots and issues seasonal notices to mariners. Bank erosion and mid-channel bar migration are continuous, and the surveyed line of the channel is revised by the operator at approximately six-month intervals.

### 4.2 Commercial river capacity

Ok Tedi Mining Limited operates the only commercial fleet on the river: eleven self-propelled barges of 1,200 to 3,000 DWT, four tugs, and two fuel barges of 1,800 tonnes capacity. The fleet is fully committed to mine inbound consumables and outbound concentrate, on a cycle of approximately eleven days. Three additional barges of 800 DWT are operated by two Daru-based coastal traders serving delta communities.

- **Endemic disease, Western Province.** Malaria holoendemic, year-round transmission of *Plasmodium falciparum* and *Plasmodium vivax*, chloroquine resistance documented, annual parasite incidence in the Middle and North Fly districts approximately 180 cases per 1,000 population. Dengue endemic at Daru and Kiunga. Scrub typhus (*Orientia tsutsugamushi*) in grassland and secondary regrowth in the Fly headwaters. Melioidosis (*Burkholderia pseudomallei*) in soil and surface water, wet-season peak. Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis at high prevalence in the Daru area. Komavi ambient conditions: mean 27 degrees Celsius, 88 percent relative humidity sustained.

- **Preventive medicine.** No force health protection policy has been issued; existing theater guidance requires malaria chemoprophylaxis, permethrin-treated uniforms, bed nets and vector control. Preventive medicine detachment support is available at Okinawa and Guam; no preventive medicine unit appears on the US Force List for Planning. Immunisation currency across notice-to-move units is 61 percent for typhoid and 34 percent for Japanese encephalitis.

- **Blood.** Armed Services Blood Program support from Yokota and Okinawa; theater liquid group O holdings 620 units, frozen holdings at Guam 1,900. Daru and Kiunga hold no bank stock.

Papua New Guinea is a party to the 1951 Convention relating to the Status of Refugees and to the 1967 Protocol, subject to reservations. Those reservations qualify Convention articles bearing on wage-earning employment, public education, freedom of movement, naturalisation, and penalties for unlawful presence and expulsion (Articles 17(1), 21, 22(1), 26, 31, 32 and 34).

The approximately 10,000 West Papuans who crossed the international border in February 2026 and settled in the Komavi area hold prima facie refugee status, recognised on a group basis by reason of the circumstances of flight rather than by individual determination.

Convention obligations attach to the contracting state, which for the Komavi population is Papua New Guinea.

Infrastructure must be constructed in order to increase coalition flow of troops and equipment; this will require an air bridge to Komavi to rapidly deploy ground troops. Our own operational COG is our ability to project forces to remote areas: a key strength relying on air capabilities, specialized forces, and logistics - to include construction capabilities. The overarching purpose of this operation is to keep/return Indonesian armed forces to their side of the international border, secure it, and then build PNG’s capacity and capability to deny OPM sanctuary, which is the root cause of the current crisis. The decisive operation is the rapid forward deployment of at least a brigade of ground troops, coordinated with PNG armed forces, to the defense of the Komavi area, supported by air. Obtaining and maintaining air superiority over the international border is decisive, as this will seriously degrade any Indonesian invasion as well as provide coalition forces protection and uninterrupted sustainment by air. Concurrent with this is the establishment of bases at Lae (Nadzab Airfield) and Dura to facilitate force flow and build critical logistics for sustainment and construction of infrastructure forward in Komvari. Special operations forces will conduct activities in Komvari in conjunction with PNG armed forces to build capacity and capability for counterinsurgency operations to deny OPM sanctuary.

OPM formed in 1965, received Libyan funding from 1969, and has since built an indigenous cadre arming disparate West Papuan groups. The National Liberation Army emerged in February 2026 as the armed wing following unification of those groups, declaring war on Indonesia to drive Indonesian forces from West Papua and shut down foreign resource extraction. The stated OPM objective is unification of West Papua with Papua New Guinea. OPM is not a designated foreign terrorist organization.

Five patterns recur: ambush of security-force convoys, including the killing of Major General I Gusti Putu Danny Karya Nugraha, head of the Papua intelligence agency, on 25 April 2021; attacks on civil aviation as the sole reliable access to the interior, the Susi Air burning of 7 February 2023 with the New Zealand pilot held until 21 September 2024 and the Smart Air killings of 11 February 2026; attacks on extractive-industry personnel, as against the Freeport Indonesia convoy on 11 February 2026; mass-casualty attacks on infrastructure workers, as at Nduga on 1 December 2018; and internationalisation of grievance through spokesman statements.

Expected behaviour is avoidance of eradication by both Indonesia and Papua New Guinea and blending with the displaced population. - **Purpose.** Compel Papua New Guinea to accept joint border security cooperation and renounce OPM sanctuary, without an acknowledged invasion and without unambiguously engaging the Australia–Papua New Guinea treaty.

Rotary-wing and short take-off and landing operations in the Fly headwaters are compressed into the 1000–1500 local window on approximately 60 percent of days, morning and late afternoon sitting below approach minima at unlit strips. Indonesian fixed-wing aviation operates from Sentani, 265 nautical miles from Komavi, with 14 hardened revetments, 8 open parking positions, and an assessed 24 to 30 sorties per day in surge, 14 sustained; attack helicopters operate from Timika, 210 nautical miles out. Indonesian Ujung Pandang Flight Information Region abuts at the meridian; there is no direct controller-to-controller coordination circuit between the two.

2.  \(E\) Commander’s initial analysis of the problem. It will take 7-10 days for sufficient naval forces to reach the area. While Lae and Port Moresby have sufficient infrastructure as APOD/SPODs, intertheater travel will be difficult. While coalition air forces can obtain air supremacy, the tropical jungle will minimize their tactical effect on either Indonesian ground troops and OPM insurgents. As well, collateral damage to PNG villages is counterproductive to U.S./PNG desired endstate. Infrastructure must be constructed in order to increase coalition flow of troops and equipment; this will require an air bridge to Komavi to rapidly deploy ground troops. Finally, the deterrence or defeat of an Indonesian invasion leaves the root cause unaddressed: OPM must be dealt with by the PNG and currently, they lack the capabilities and equipment to do this. Local sympathies also rest with the separatists as the Komavi peoples straddle both sides of the border. In order to deny OPM sanctuary in the future, sympathies and local support has to change. Our own operational COG is our ability to project forces to remote areas: a key strength relying on air capabilities, specialized forces, and logistics - to include construction capabilities. We are vulnerable, however, in the area of force protection: our troops and equipment simply are not well-acclimated to the region and there is little time in which to get them acclimated.

### 8.1 Effects on materiel and personnel

Heat, heavy rain and high humidity degrade supplies, equipment and troops at a high rate. Documented effects in this environment include fungal growth on optics and electrical insulation within 14 days of exposure; corrosion of unprotected ferrous components within 30 days; degradation of packaged rations and medical stores held outside climate control; saturation of textiles and leather that does not reverse without forced drying; and reduced service life of rotary-wing dynamic components from ingested moisture and particulate.

Personnel not acclimatised to a sustained wet-bulb globe temperature in the range experienced in the Fly lowland require a phased acclimatisation period, during which work-rest cycles and water intake requirements are substantially more restrictive than in temperate conditions. The 1942 to 1944 campaign in Papua New Guinea produced more casualties from weather and terrain than from combat.

- **Endemic disease, Western Province.** Malaria holoendemic, year-round transmission of *Plasmodium falciparum* and *Plasmodium vivax*, chloroquine resistance documented, annual parasite incidence in the Middle and North Fly districts approximately 180 cases per 1,000 population. Dengue endemic at Daru and Kiunga. Scrub typhus (*Orientia tsutsugamushi*) in grassland and secondary regrowth in the Fly headwaters. Melioidosis (*Burkholderia pseudomallei*) in soil and surface water, wet-season peak. Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis at high prevalence in the Daru area. Komavi ambient conditions: mean 27 degrees Celsius, 88 percent relative humidity sustained.

- **Preventive medicine.** No force health protection policy has been issued; existing theater guidance requires malaria chemoprophylaxis, permethrin-treated uniforms, bed nets and vector control. Preventive medicine detachment support is available at Okinawa and Guam; no preventive medicine unit appears on the US Force List for Planning. Immunisation currency across notice-to-move units is 61 percent for typhoid and 34 percent for Japanese encephalitis.
